lessons.title: Lesson 1: The three duties: care, loyalty and obedience
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the board's three core duties and spot when one is at risk.
This lesson builds toward: Given a board decision or situation, you will explain the duties of care, loyalty and obedience and identify which duty is at risk, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Board members of a nonprofit hold the organization in trust for the public and the people it serves. That trust is often described as three duties.
Duty of care: pay attention and make informed decisions. Come to meetings, read the reports, ask questions, and use good judgment. Duty of loyalty: put the organization's interests ahead of your own, and never use your seat to benefit yourself, your family or your business. Duty of obedience: make sure the organization follows its mission, its own bylaws and the law.
These duties belong to every board member, not only the chair or the treasurer. "I didn't read the budget" is not an excuse. Exact legal rules vary by state, so ask a nonprofit lawyer when a decision is serious.
Words to know:
- Board of directors: the group legally responsible for overseeing a nonprofit.
- Fiduciary duty: a legal duty to act in someone else's best interest; board members owe it to the organization.
- Duty of care: making informed, careful decisions.
- Duty of loyalty: putting the organization's interests ahead of your own.
- Duty of obedience: keeping the organization true to its mission, bylaws and the law.
Try it now: Write one real example of each duty for a nonprofit you know, such as a food bank, church or youth sports league. Then write one action that would break each duty.
You can now explain the duties of care, loyalty and obedience and spot when one is at risk.

check.q: What does the duty of loyalty ask of a board member?
options: Come to every meeting on time
Follow the bylaws and the law
Put the organization's interests ahead of your own
Raise the most money
check.why: Loyalty means never using your seat to benefit yourself, your family or your business.

check.q: A member says, "I don't read the reports; the treasurer handles money." What do you tell them?
options: Every member has the duty of care, so read the reports and ask questions
That is fine; only the treasurer is responsible
Ask staff to vote for you
Skip money votes
check.why: The three duties belong to every board member, and not reading the budget is no excuse.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Board and staff roles, and the bylaws
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Split common decisions between board and staff and find the key rules in your bylaws.
This lesson builds toward: Using your bylaws and a skills grid, you will divide common decisions between board and staff, find the key rules in the bylaws, and plan how to fill open board seats, with five decisions sorted and two seats matched to skill gaps.
In most nonprofits with paid staff, the board sets direction and oversees; staff run the daily work. The board approves the mission, strategy and budget, hires, supports and reviews the executive director, watches the money and risks, and helps raise funds. The executive director runs programs, hires and manages other staff, and makes daily decisions.
Problems start when a board micromanages staff, or when a board rubber-stamps everything without asking questions. In small, all-volunteer groups, board members often also do hands-on work, so be clear about which "hat" you are wearing.
Bylaws are the organization's own rule book. They usually set the number of board members, how they are elected and for how long, the officers, how meetings are called, how many members make a quorum, and how votes work. Keep a current copy, read it, and follow it. Change bylaws only by the process they describe.
Step by step:
- List five common decisions (budget, hiring staff, a new program, a big contract, an event date).
- Mark each as board, staff or both.
- Open your bylaws and find: board size, terms, officers, quorum and voting rules.
- Note anything your board is not following.
Words to know:
- Executive director: the top staff leader who runs the nonprofit day to day and reports to the board.
- Bylaws: the nonprofit's rules for how the board and organization work.
- Quorum: the minimum number of members who must be present for a meeting to make decisions.
- Micromanage: to control small details of someone else's work.
Try it now: Get your organization's bylaws (or a sample from a nonprofit you know). Find the board size, term length, quorum and how votes are taken. Then sort five common decisions into board, staff or both.
You can now keep board and staff roles clear and find the key rules in a set of bylaws.

options: The state's tax rules
The executive director's job description
A list of donors
The organization's own rule book, such as board size, terms, quorum and voting
check.why: Bylaws are the organization's own rules for how the board works.

check.q: The board chair starts telling program staff how to run each daily activity. What is the problem?
options: Nothing; the chair runs daily work
The board is micromanaging; daily work belongs to staff led by the executive director
The chair should also do payroll
Staff should vote on the budget instead
check.why: The board sets direction and oversees; staff run the daily work.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Board meetings and minutes
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Run a board meeting that follows the bylaws and record clear minutes.
This lesson builds toward: For an upcoming board meeting, you will write an agenda with a consent agenda and record minutes with attendance, quorum, motions, votes and actions, with every required part of the minutes.
Send the agenda and reports at least several days ahead so members can prepare. Many boards use a consent agenda for routine items (like approving last meeting's minutes) so they can spend time on the big questions.
Check that you have a quorum before voting. For each decision, someone makes a motion, the board discusses it, and the chair calls a vote. Members with a conflict of interest step out of the discussion and vote.
Minutes are the official record. They list the date, who was present, whether there was a quorum, each motion and the result of the vote, any conflicts declared, and actions with owners. Keep them short and factual; they are not a word-for-word transcript. Approve them at the next meeting and keep them safe.
Step by step:
- Send the agenda and reports days ahead.
- Use a consent agenda for routine items.
- Confirm a quorum before any vote.
- For each decision: motion, discussion, vote.
- Record minutes: date, attendance, quorum, motions, votes, conflicts, actions.
- Approve minutes at the next meeting and store them safely.
Words to know:
- Minutes: the official written record of what a board decided at a meeting.
- Motion: a formal proposal for the board to vote on.
- Consent agenda: a group of routine items approved with one vote.
Try it now: Write a one-page board meeting agenda with a consent agenda section and two discussion items. Then write sample minutes for one motion, including who moved it, the vote count and the result.
You can now run a board meeting that follows the rules and record clear, official minutes.

options: A word-for-word transcript of everything said
The official, short and factual record of the meeting
The agenda sent before the meeting
A list of members' phone numbers
check.why: Minutes are the official record: who was there, quorum, motions, votes, conflicts and actions.

check.q: Only a few members arrive and you are not sure you can vote. What do you check first?
options: Whether the coffee is ready
Whether the minutes are long enough
Whether staff agree
Whether there is a quorum under the bylaws
check.why: The board can only make decisions when a quorum is present.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Handling conflicts of interest
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Follow clear steps when a board member has a conflict of interest.
This lesson builds toward: When a board member or their family or business could gain from a decision, you will follow the conflict-of-interest steps: disclose, step out, check the deal is fair and record it, in the right order and recorded in the minutes.
A conflict of interest happens when a board member, or their family or business, could gain from a decision the board makes. Conflicts are common in small communities and are not always wrong, but they must be handled openly.
Most boards adopt a written conflict-of-interest policy and ask members to sign a yearly disclosure form. When a conflict comes up: the member tells the board, leaves the discussion and the vote, and the board decides whether the deal is fair to the organization, ideally after comparing other options. The minutes record all of this.
Example: the treasurer's cousin runs a printing shop that bids on the annual report. The treasurer discloses it and steps out; the board compares three quotes and picks the best value. Transactions with insiders can have tax and legal consequences, so get advice from a lawyer or accountant on anything large.
Step by step:
- Adopt a written conflict-of-interest policy.
- Collect a signed disclosure form from each member every year.
- When a conflict arises, the member discloses it.
- The member leaves the discussion and vote.
- The board checks the deal is fair, ideally by comparing options.
- Record it all in the minutes; get advice on large deals.
Words to know:
- Conflict of interest: when a person's own interests could affect a decision they make for the organization.
- Disclosure: openly telling the board about a possible conflict.
- Recuse: to step out of a discussion and vote because of a conflict.
Try it now: Write the five steps your board will follow when a conflict comes up, in plain words. Then apply them to this case: a board member's spouse wants to sell the nonprofit a used van.
You can now handle a conflict of interest with disclosure, recusal, a fair review and a written record.

check.q: When does a conflict of interest happen?
options: When a member, their family or their business could gain from a board decision
When two members disagree
When a meeting runs late
When the budget is tight
check.why: A conflict exists when someone on the board could personally gain from the decision.

check.q: A member's sister runs the catering company bidding on your gala. What happens next?
options: The member votes, since family helps
Hide it from the minutes
The member discloses it and steps out, and the board compares quotes
Cancel the gala
check.why: The member discloses and leaves the discussion and vote, and the board checks the deal is fair.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Financial oversight, Form 990 and state registration
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Review a nonprofit's finances as a board member and put the yearly filings on a calendar.
This lesson builds toward: Given a nonprofit's income, assets and year-end date, you will review its financial reports and build a yearly calendar of its Form 990 and state filings, with the version and due date confirmed on irs.gov and the state charity office's site.
Every board member, not just the treasurer, should understand the basics: the approved budget, regular reports comparing actual income and spending to the budget, the balance sheet (what the organization owns and owes), cash on hand, and any restricted gifts that must be used for a specific purpose. Ask questions when numbers change a lot. Use controls like two people involved in paying bills, and an outside review or audit when the size of the organization calls for it.
Most tax-exempt organizations must file an annual return with the IRS from the Form 990 series. The IRS says organizations whose gross receipts are normally $50,000 or less can file the Form 990-N e-Postcard; those with gross receipts under $200,000 and total assets under $500,000 can file Form 990-EZ or Form 990; larger ones file Form 990. The return is due on the 15th day of the 5th month after the year ends (May 15 for a December 31 year). The IRS says organizations that do not file for three years in a row automatically lose their tax-exempt status. These returns must also be made available to the public. Thresholds and rules can change, so check irs.gov each year. Churches and some other groups have different rules.
States have their own rules. In California, the Attorney General's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers requires charities to register and file annual reports, with limited exceptions. Check oag.ca.gov/charities for current forms and fees. Other states have their own charity offices. Have an accountant help prepare filings, and the board should review them before they are filed.
Step by step:
- Approve a yearly budget.
- Review budget-versus-actual reports at each meeting.
- Check cash, the balance sheet and restricted gifts.
- Use controls: two people on payments; an outside review when needed.
- Put the Form 990 due date on the calendar; confirm which version on irs.gov.
- Put state filings on the calendar (California: oag.ca.gov/charities).
- Review filings before they are sent; get an accountant's help.
Words to know:
- Budget versus actual: a report comparing planned income and spending with what really happened.
- Balance sheet: a report of what an organization owns and owes on a date.
- Restricted gift: a donation that must be used for a specific purpose.
- Form 990: the IRS annual information return for most tax-exempt organizations.
- Registry of Charities and Fundraisers: the California Attorney General's office where charities register and file annual reports.
Official sources:
- IRS: Form 990 series, which forms do exempt organizations file
- IRS: Return due dates for exempt organizations
- IRS: Automatic revocation of exemption
- IRS: Public disclosure of exempt organization returns
- California Attorney General: Registry of Charities and Fundraisers
- California Attorney General's Guide for Charities (PDF)
Try it now: Look up a nonprofit you know on a public database or in its annual report. Note its approximate yearly income and decide which Form 990 version it likely files, then confirm the rule on irs.gov. Write its Form 990 due date and, if it is in California, its Registry renewal on a yearly calendar.
You can now review a nonprofit's finances as a board member and plan its yearly IRS and state filings.

check.q: What does a balance sheet show?
options: Who came to the meeting
The board's term limits
Next year's events
What the organization owns and owes
check.why: The balance sheet shows what the organization owns and owes.

check.q: Your nonprofit's year ends December 31. What do you put on the board calendar?
options: Nothing; filings are optional
The Form 990 due date of May 15, after confirming the version on irs.gov
A reminder to file every five years
Only the holiday party
check.why: The return is due on the 15th day of the 5th month after the year ends, and the version is confirmed on irs.gov.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Recruiting and welcoming board members
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a skills grid to recruit the board members your nonprofit needs.
This lesson builds toward: Using your bylaws and a skills grid, you will divide common decisions between board and staff, find the key rules in the bylaws, and plan how to fill open board seats, with five decisions sorted and two seats matched to skill gaps.
Recruit on purpose, not only from friends. Make a skills grid: list the skills and connections your board needs (for example finance, law, fundraising, the community you serve, technology) and mark which current members have them. The gaps tell you who to look for. Include people with lived experience of the issue you work on.
Be honest about the job: how many meetings, what committees, how much time, and the expectation to give or help raise money, if there is one. Meet candidates more than once, have them attend a meeting, and check references. Elect them by the process in your bylaws.
Welcome new members with an orientation: the mission, bylaws, budget and latest financial report, recent minutes, the conflict-of-interest policy to sign, and a board buddy. Review the board's own work every year, and use term limits so new people keep joining.
Step by step:
- Build a skills grid; find the gaps.
- Look beyond friends; include lived experience.
- Write an honest description of the role and time.
- Meet candidates, invite them to a meeting, check references.
- Elect by the bylaws' process.
- Hold an orientation and assign a board buddy.
- Review the board every year.
Words to know:
- Skills grid: a chart of the skills a board needs and which members have them.
- Orientation: the welcome and training a new member gets.
- Term limit: a cap on how many terms a person can serve in a row.
Try it now: Final task: build your one-page governance checklist. Include the three duties, a board-versus-staff split for five decisions, a meeting agenda and minutes template, conflict-of-interest steps, a yearly filing and finance calendar, and a recruiting plan for two seats from a skills grid.
You can now recruit and welcome board members who fill real gaps, and keep the board healthy year after year.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds The three duties A duty is missing or explained wrongly. Care, loyalty and obedience are each explained in plain words. Each duty has a real example of keeping it and breaking it. Roles and recruiting Decisions are not sorted, or recruiting is from friends only. Five decisions sorted into board, staff or both, and two open seats matched to gaps in a skills grid. Also notes bylaw rules the board is not following and an orientation plan for new members. Meetings and minutes No agenda, or minutes miss quorum, motions or votes. An agenda with a consent agenda and a minutes template with every required part. Sample minutes for one motion with who moved it, the vote count and the result. Conflict of interest Steps are missing or out of order. Disclose, step out, check the deal is fair, and record it, in order. Also includes the yearly signed disclosure form and when to get legal advice. Finance and filing calendar No Form 990 version or due date, or no state filing. Budget reviews, the right Form 990 version and due date, and any state registration, confirmed on official sites. Also lists financial controls such as two people on payments, and names where each rule was checked. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does a skills grid show?
options: Members' birthdays
The meeting schedule
The skills and connections the board needs, and which members have them
The yearly budget
check.why: A skills grid shows the gaps, which tells you who to recruit.

check.q: Your grid shows no one with finance skills. What is a good next step?
options: Look beyond friends for a candidate with finance skills, meet them and invite them to a meeting
Ask your best friend, whatever their skills
Leave the gap; it does not matter
Make the treasurer do everything
check.why: Recruit on purpose to fill gaps, and meet candidates and have them attend a meeting first.
